Even though everyone tries to tell me it's not true, I can't shake the conviction that it's actually happening. My experiences are really just limited to that constant, unsettling feeling of being watched by the cameras on the unit and the mirrors at home.\n\nDoctor: Can you confirm again if you have ever experienced any hallucinations, such as hearing voices or seeing things that others cannot, separate from your beliefs about being watched?\n\nPatient: No, I can definitely confirm that I have never heard any voices or seen things that aren't actually there. My main concern is really just that constant, unsettling feeling of being watched by the cameras on the unit and the mirrors at home.\n\nDoctor: Have you ever experienced any periods where you felt like you were in a different reality or had a break from reality, where things seemed unreal or distant to you?\n\nPatient: Yes, I definitely feel like I'm in a different reality when I believe the hospital cameras and my mirrors at home are watching me as part of an experiment. My thoughts also jump all over the place during those times, and I'll suddenly feel like the colors in my murals are spying on me, which makes everything feel very unreal.\n\nDoctor: Can you tell me if you think the colors in your murals are actually spying on you, or if that's just a feeling you have when you're in that different reality?\n\nPatient: When my thoughts start jumping all over the place, it genuinely feels like the colors in the murals are spying on me, making it feel like a real occurrence instead of just a passing feeling. I notice it really confuses people when I try to explain it, but to me, it feels completely real in those moments.\n\nDoctor: Can you clarify if you've ever heard voices or seen things that others cannot, in addition to your beliefs about being watched and the hospital experimenting on you?\n\nPatient: No, I haven't heard any voices or seen things that aren't actually there. My main concern is really just that constant, unsettling feeling of being watched through the cameras on the unit and the mirrors at home.\n\nDoctor: Can you describe how you distinguish between what feels real to you, like being watched, and what others tell you is not real, and do you ever have moments where you question your own perceptions of reality?\n\nPatient: Even though people constantly tell me the cameras and mirrors aren't watching me, it feels completely real and impossible to shake. The feeling that the hospital is running an experiment on my mind is so strong that I can't help but believe it. Because of that, it's very hard for me to trust or agree with what others say is \"real.\"\n\nDoctor: Can you tell me if you've ever experienced any times where you felt like you were completely normal and not being watched, without any of these paranoid thoughts, even if it was just for a short period?\n\nPatient: I haven't really had any times where I felt completely normal since all of this started. Even during those brief weeks when the thoughts about being watched backed off a bit, that heavy, numb depression was still constantly there and never really let up.\n\nDoctor: Can you clarify if you believe the thoughts about being watched and the hospital experimenting on you are based on any actual events or evidence, or if they just feel true to you without any basis in reality?\n\nPatient: The cameras on the unit and the mirrors at home feel like direct evidence to me that I'm being watched and experimented on. Even though everyone tries to tell me it's not true, I can't shake the conviction that it's actually happening. It just feels completely real and true to me.\n\nDoctor: Can you tell me if you have ever experienced any prominent hallucinations, such as hearing voices or seeing things that others cannot, in addition to your delusional thoughts about being watched?\n\nPatient: No, I have never heard any voices or seen things that other people couldn't see. My experiences are really just limited to that constant, unsettling feeling of being watched by the cameras on the unit and the mirrors at home.\n\nDoctor: Can you confirm again if you have ever experienced any hallucinations, such as hearing voices or seeing things that others cannot, separate from your beliefs about being watched?\n\nPatient: No, I can definitely confirm that I have never heard any voices or seen things that aren't actually there. My main experience of that nature is just the really strong, unsettling feeling of being watched by the cameras on the unit and the mirrors at home.\n\nDoctor: Can you describe how your beliefs about being watched and the hospital experimenting on you relate to your feelings of heaviness, emptiness, and exhaustion, and do you think one causes the other or if they are separate issues for you?\n\nPatient: On my worst days, they hit me at the exact same time, so I feel completely empty and exhausted while also believing the cameras and mirrors are tracking me. But they can also be separate, like a few months ago when my mood just felt flat rather than deeply sad, yet I was still convinced they were recording my thoughts.\n\nDoctor: Do you think your feelings of heaviness, emptiness, and exhaustion would improve if your beliefs about being watched and the hospital experimenting on you were to somehow be proven false or alleviated?\n\nPatient: I don't think resolving those thoughts about the cameras would really lift this heavy, empty feeling. Even during the times when the ideas about being watched back off a bit, the numb depression and exhaustion still remain just as strong and haven't let up at all.\n\nDoctor: Can you describe if there are any specific triggers or situations that make your beliefs about being watched or the hospital experimenting on you feel more intense or real to you?\n\nPatient: I'm not really sure about any specific triggers, other than just being around the cameras on the unit or looking at the mirrors at home. For the most part, that unsettling feeling of being watched is just constantly there in the background.\n\nDoctor: Can you describe if your beliefs about being watched and the hospital experimenting on you have ever changed or wavered over time, or if they have remained consistent and unshakeable?\n\nPatient: These beliefs have been around for about a year now, and they are generally very persistent and unshakeable. There are some weeks where the thoughts back off a bit or feel slightly less intense, but they never really go away. Even when everyone tries to convince me it isn't true, I still can't shake the feeling.\n\nDoctor: Can you tell me if you have ever experienced any periods where you felt like you had special powers, were on a mission, or had grandiose ideas about yourself, in addition to your beliefs about being watched?\n\nPatient: No, I have never felt like I had special powers or any kind of grand mission. My experiences are really just limited to feeling watched by the cameras and mirrors, and that heavy, empty mood.\n\nDoctor: Can you tell me if you have ever experienced any episodes of mania or hypomania, where you felt extremely happy, energetic, or irritable, and had decreased need for sleep, or if your mood has primarily been low and depressive?\n\nPatient: No, I have never had any periods where I felt extremely happy, energetic, or hyperactive. My mood has always been low and depressive, and I just feel completely weighed down and exhausted instead of full of energy.\n\nDoctor: Can you confirm if you have ever experienced any periods where you had both delusions of being watched and hallucinations, such as hearing voices, at the same time?\n\nPatient: No, I've never experienced both because I have never had any hallucinations. Even during times when the thoughts about the cameras and mirrors backed off a bit, the numb depression and the feeling of dragging a heavy weight never really let up. I'd still just feel completely empty inside.\n\nDoctor: Do you think your beliefs about being watched and the hospital experimenting on you are more distressing to you, or is the heavy, empty mood and exhaustion more bothersome to you on a daily basis?"

While the terrifying belief about the cameras and mirrors watching me is incredibly intense and frightening, those thoughts sometimes back off slightly, whereas the depression is always there.

This has been going on for a little over a year now, right along with that heavy mood.\n\nDoctor: Have you experienced any periods over the past year where your mood and energy levels improved for at least a couple of months before returning to this heavy, empty state, or has it been consistently present since it started?\n\nPatient: No, I haven't had any long periods of improvement like that; it has been consistently heavy and empty almost the entire time. There was only a brief stretch a few months ago, for maybe a couple of weeks, where my mood felt more flat than deeply sad, but otherwise the heavy depression has never really let up.\n\nDoctor: Can you tell me more about that brief period a few months ago when your mood felt more flat than deeply sad - did you experience any significant changes in your sleep patterns, appetite, or concentration during that time?\n\nPatient: During those couple of weeks, my mood was just flat, but I was still really fixated on the idea that the cameras on the unit were watching me. As for things like my sleep, appetite, or concentration during that specific time, I'm really not sure and don't quite remember if they changed.\n\nDoctor: You mentioned being fixated on the idea that cameras were watching you during that brief period - have you experienced any other thoughts like that, where you felt like you were being followed, heard voices, or had similar paranoid thoughts?\n\nPatient: I haven't heard any voices, but I'm convinced the mirrors at home are watching me too, and that the hospital is running some kind of experiment on my mind with everyone in on it. Sometimes it even feels like the colors in the murals are spying on me, and it's hard to make sense of it all.\n\nDoctor: Can you tell me more about when these thoughts about being watched and the hospital experimenting on you started, and how long you've been experiencing them?\n\nPatient: Those thoughts started about a year ago, shortly after the stress from the extra night shifts really began to build up. They have been hanging around in one form or another for about a year now, and I just can't seem to shake them.\n\nDoctor: Can you describe how these thoughts of being watched and the hospital experimenting on you affect your daily life and interactions with others, and do you think these thoughts are real or possibly a product of your own mind?\n\nPatient: Believing I'm being watched makes me so paranoid and exhausted that I've been calling out of work, avoiding my friends, and letting all my chores at home slide. As for whether it's real, it feels completely real to me, and even though people keep telling me otherwise, I can't shake the feeling that it's actually happening.\n\nDoctor: Do you think these beliefs about being watched and the hospital experimenting on you are true, even if others tell you they are not, and do you feel like you have any control over these thoughts?\n\nPatient: Yes, I absolutely believe it is true because it feels completely real to me, no matter how many times people tell me otherwise. I don't have any control over these thoughts at all; they just completely take over my mind and I can't stop them.\n\nDoctor: Can you describe a specific situation where your belief in being watched or the hospital experimenting on you led to a behavior or action that significantly impacted your life or relationships, and how you felt about it afterwards?\n\nPatient: I'm not really sure how to answer that, and I can't think of one specific event where I took action because of it. It's more just a constant, heavy dread that makes me want to isolate myself from everyone.\n\nDoctor: You've mentioned believing in being watched and that the hospital is experimenting on you, which feels very real to you. Can you tell me if you've ever had any experiences where you thought someone or something was inserting thoughts into your mind or controlling your actions?\n\nPatient: No, I haven't experienced anything like having thoughts put into my mind or having my actions controlled by someone else. My thoughts also jump all over the place during those times, and I'll suddenly feel like the colors in my murals are spying on me, which makes everything feel very unreal.\n\nDoctor: Can you tell me if you think the colors in your murals are actually spying on you, or if that's just a feeling you have when you're in that different reality?\n\nPatient: When my thoughts start jumping all over the place, it genuinely feels like the colors in the murals are spying on me, making it feel like a real occurrence instead of just a passing feeling. My main concern is really just that constant, unsettling feeling of being watched through the cameras on the unit and the mirrors at home.\n\nDoctor: Can you describe how you distinguish between what feels real to you, like being watched, and what others tell you is not real, and do you ever have moments where you question your own perceptions of reality?\n\nPatient: Even though people constantly tell me the cameras and mirrors aren't watching me, it feels completely real and impossible to shake. Even during those brief weeks when the thoughts about being watched backed off a bit, that heavy, numb depression was still constantly there and never really let up.\n\nDoctor: Can you clarify if you believe the thoughts about being watched and the hospital experimenting on you are based on any actual events or evidence, or if they just feel true to you without any basis in reality?\n\nPatient: The cameras on the unit and the mirrors at home feel like direct evidence to me that I'm being watched and experimented on. Even though everyone tries to tell me it's not true, I can't shake the conviction that it's actually happening. It just feels completely real and true to me.\n\nDoctor: Can you tell me if you have ever experienced any prominent hallucinations, such as hearing voices or seeing things that others cannot, in addition to your delusional thoughts about being watched?\n\nPatient: No, I have never heard any voices or seen things that other people couldn't see. My experiences are really just limited to that constant, unsettling feeling of being watched by the cameras on the unit and the mirrors at home.\n\nDoctor: Can you confirm again if you have ever experienced any hallucinations, such as hearing voices or seeing things that others cannot, separate from your beliefs about being watched?\n\nPatient: No, I can definitely confirm that I have never heard any voices or seen things that aren't actually there. My main experience of that nature is just the really strong, unsettling feeling of being watched by the cameras on the unit and the mirrors at home.\n\nDoctor: Can you describe how your beliefs about being watched and the hospital experimenting on you relate to your feelings of heaviness, emptiness, and exhaustion, and do you think one causes the other or if they are separate issues for you?\n\nPatient: On my worst days, they hit me at the exact same time, so I feel completely empty and exhausted while also believing the cameras and mirrors are tracking me. Even during the times when the ideas about being watched back off a bit, the numb depression and exhaustion still remain just as strong and haven't let up at all.\n\nDoctor: Can you describe if there are any specific triggers or situations that make your beliefs about being watched or the hospital experimenting on you feel more intense or real to you?\n\nPatient: I'm not really sure about any specific triggers, other than just being around the cameras on the unit or looking at the mirrors at home. There are some weeks where the thoughts back off a bit or feel slightly less intense, but they never really go away. Even when everyone tries to convince me it isn't true, I still can't shake the feeling.\n\nDoctor: Can you tell me if you have ever experienced any periods where you felt like you had special powers, were on a mission, or had grandiose ideas about yourself, in addition to your beliefs about being watched?\n\nPatient: No, I have never felt like I had special powers or any kind of grand mission.
